Robust, quantile, GAM and kernel alternatives

Source: vignettes/v08-flexible-alternatives.Rmd
v08-flexible-alternatives.Rmd

Alternatives should answer a diagnosed problem

A flexible model is not automatically better than OLS. Different alternatives address different departures:

  • robust regression reduces the influence of unusual observations;
  • quantile regression changes the target from the conditional mean to a conditional quantile;
  • GAM relaxes linear functional forms while retaining an additive structure;
  • kernel regression provides a more nonparametric conditional-mean estimate.

The first task is therefore to identify why an alternative is scientifically useful.

Robust regression: soil example 

soil <- mr_example_data("soil_fertility")
ols_soil <- mr_fit(
  yield_t_ha ~ soil_pH + organic_matter_pct + available_P_mg_dm3 +
    season_rain_mm,
  soil
)
rob_soil <- mr_fit(
  yield_t_ha ~ soil_pH + organic_matter_pct + available_P_mg_dm3 +
    season_rain_mm,
  soil,
  engine = "robust"
)
cbind(OLS = coef(ols_soil), Robust = coef(rob_soil))
#>                             OLS       Robust
#> (Intercept)         2.836102671  2.782495152
#> soil_pH            -0.030783358 -0.017146631
#> organic_matter_pct  0.162433941  0.154313238
#> available_P_mg_dm3  0.028151382  0.028197622
#> season_rain_mm      0.003373274  0.003360978

Robust regression is best interpreted as a sensitivity analysis when unusual observations may disproportionately affect OLS. It should not be used to hide valid observations simply because they disagree with the dominant trend.

Robust regression: plant example 

plant <- mr_example_data("plant_growth")
rob_plant <- mr_fit(
  biomass_g ~ leaf_area_cm2 + chlorophyll_spad + leaf_N_pct +
    stomatal_conductance + plant_height_cm,
  plant,
  engine = "robust"
)
summary(rob_plant)

Quantile regression: low, median and high yield 

het <- mr_example_data("agronomy_heteroskedastic")
base_het <- mr_fit(
  grain_yield_t_ha ~ N_rate_kg_ha + P_rate_kg_ha + soil_water_m3_m3,
  het
)
if (requireNamespace("quantreg", quietly = TRUE)) {
  q25 <- mr_quantile(base_het, tau = 0.25)
  q50 <- mr_quantile(base_het, tau = 0.50)
  q75 <- mr_quantile(base_het, tau = 0.75)
  coef(q25$model)
  coef(q50$model)
  coef(q75$model)
}
#>      (Intercept)     N_rate_kg_ha     P_rate_kg_ha soil_water_m3_m3 
#>       3.70056616       0.03200682       0.04030795       4.00816841

The three calls demonstrate that mr_quantile() can be used for distinct conditional response levels. A single multi-quantile fit is also available.

if (requireNamespace("quantreg", quietly = TRUE)) {
  q_all <- mr_quantile(base_het, tau = c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9))
  summary(q_all$model)
}

Quantile-specific slopes can be agronomically relevant when nutrient or water responses differ between stressed and high-performing environments.

Detect nonlinear irrigation response 

nl <- mr_example_data("irrigation_nonlinear")
lin <- mr_fit(
  yield_t_ha ~ irrigation_mm + N_rate_kg_ha + mean_temp_C,
  nl,
  goal = "prediction"
)
mr_diagnose(lin)$specification
#>   statistic         df1         df2     p.value 
#>   0.7537816   2.0000000 164.0000000   0.4722068

GAM: interpretable smooth effects 

gam1 <- mr_fit(
  yield_t_ha ~ s(irrigation_mm) + s(N_rate_kg_ha) + s(mean_temp_C),
  nl,
  engine = "gam",
  goal = "prediction"
)
summary(gam1)

Estimated smooth response functions in the irrigation GAM.

A second GAM can retain one linear agronomic term and smooth only the variables with plausible nonlinear response.

gam2 <- mr_fit(
  yield_t_ha ~ s(irrigation_mm) + N_rate_kg_ha + s(mean_temp_C) +
    plant_stand_plants_m2,
  nl,
  engine = "gam",
  goal = "prediction"
)
summary(gam2)

Kernel regression

Kernel regression is useful when the functional form is difficult to specify. Bandwidth selection is part of the model and can be computationally expensive. The following three examples are kept unevaluated during vignette building to avoid long package-installation times; the package validation script executes them separately.

ker1 <- mr_kernel(lin)
ker1$bandwidth
lin_two <- mr_fit(yield_t_ha ~ irrigation_mm + N_rate_kg_ha, nl)
ker2 <- mr_kernel(lin_two)
ker2$model
lin_temp <- mr_fit(yield_t_ha ~ irrigation_mm + mean_temp_C, nl)
ker3 <- mr_kernel(lin_temp, bwmethod = "cv.aic")
ker3$bandwidth

Compare OLS, GAM and kernel out of sample 

ker_fit <- mr_fit(
  yield_t_ha ~ irrigation_mm + N_rate_kg_ha + mean_temp_C,
  nl,
  engine = "kernel",
  goal = "prediction"
)
mr_compare(linear = lin, gam = gam1, kernel = ker_fit,
           v = 5, repeats = 3, seed = 91)$prediction

The comparison must use out-of-fold predictions. A flexible model can always fit training data more closely, but that is not enough to demonstrate improved prediction.

Choosing among alternatives

Use robust regression when the main concern is sensitivity to influential observations. Use quantile regression when the scientific target is a conditional quantile. Use GAM when smooth nonlinear functional forms are plausible and interpretability remains important. Use kernel regression when a less structured conditional-mean estimate is justified and sample size supports it.

A single dataset may motivate more than one sensitivity analysis, but every additional model should correspond to an explicit scientific or diagnostic question.
